title: A & V Pattern Strabismus: The Incomitant Enigma
summary: A and V pattern strabismus represent common forms of incomitant horizontal deviations, characterized by a significant change in deviation magnitude between upgaze and downgaze. Understanding these patterns is crucial for accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and achieving optimal ocular alignment and binocular function.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: A and V patterns are types of incomitant strabismus where the horizontal deviation (esotropia or exotropia) changes significantly with vertical gaze. An **A-pattern** indicates that the eyes are more convergent (less divergent) in upgaze and more divergent (less convergent) in downgaze. A **V-pattern** indicates the eyes are more divergent (less convergent) in upgaze and more convergent (less divergent) in downgaze. These patterns are clinically significant when the difference in horizontal deviation between upgaze and downgaze is ≥10 prism diopters (PD) for A-patterns or ≥15 PD for V-patterns.

branches: - V-pattern: Inferior oblique (IO) overaction OR Superior oblique (SO) underaction.
- A-pattern: SO overaction OR IO underaction.
- Abnormal vertical insertion of horizontal recti (e.g., medial rectus inserted superiorly, lateral rectus inserted inferiorly for V-pattern).
- Anomalies like craniosynostosis can affect muscle pulley positions.
- Aberrant supranuclear input to vertical gaze centers affecting horizontal recti.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: **Cosmetic Deviation:** Most common complaint, visible eye misalignment.
**Abnormal Head Posture:** Chin-up or chin-down to achieve binocularity (e.g., chin-up for V-exo to avoid diplopia in downgaze).
**Diplopia:** Especially in extreme up or down gazes where fusion cannot be maintained.
**Asthenopia:** Eye strain, headaches.
**Reading Difficulties:** More common with A-patterns, where convergence demand in downgaze (reading position) is higher in esotropia or divergence is greater in exotropia.
**Amblyopia/Suppression:** Particularly in young children with constant deviation.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **Primary Gaze Deviation:** Measured by PACT.
**Deviations in Up/Down Gaze:** Crucial measurements via PACT at 25-30° upgaze and downgaze.
**Oblique Muscle Function Assessment:** Evaluate superior and inferior oblique over/underaction (e.g., Bielschowsky head tilt test if vertical component is significant).

**Fundus Torsion:** Indirect sign of oblique muscle dysfunction; extorsion with IO overaction/SO underaction (V-pattern), intorsion with SO overaction/IO underaction (A-pattern). Assessed via indirect ophthalmoscopy or fundus photography (disk-fovea relationship).
**Version/Duction Abnormalities:** Restricted movements or overactions in specific gazes.
**Vertical Incomitance:** Associated vertical deviation that also changes with gaze.

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic Exam** – Visual acuity, refraction, cycloplegic refraction, slit-lamp, fundus exam.

**Step 2: Prism and Alternate Cover Test (PACT)** – Performed in primary gaze, 25-30° upgaze, and 25-30° downgaze. Crucial for quantifying the pattern. May also be performed in the 8 diagnostic gazes if there are significant horizontal incomitances.

**Step 3: Assessment of Oblique Muscle Function** – Observations of torsional movements, elevation/depression in adduction. Measure oblique over/underactions from +1 to +4 (overaction) or -1 to -4 (underaction).
**Step 4: Forced Duction Test (FDT)** – If restrictive strabismus is suspected (e.g., thyroid eye disease, orbital mass). Performed under topical anesthesia with forceps to passively move the globe.
**Step 5: Active Force Generation Test (AFGT)** – Rarely used; assesses muscle strength in cases of paresis.
**Step 6: Motor Fields (Lees/Hess Charts)** – Graphical representation of eye movements, useful for documenting incomitance.
**Step 7: Neuroimaging (CT/MRI)** – If acute onset, associated neurological symptoms, or suspicion of orbital pathology/cranial nerve palsy.

rows: Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, VI)
Acute onset, specific muscle paralysis/paresis, large primary/secondary deviation, gaze restriction.
Typically affects all gaze directions, not just vertical extremes, and often with significant vertical deviation.
Restrictive Strabismus (e.g., Thyroid Eye Disease, Orbital Fracture, Duane's Syndrome)
Positive Forced Duction Test, limited range of motion, specific history (trauma, autoimmune).
May mimic patterns due to mechanical restriction, but FDT is key.
Skew Deviation
Associated with central neurological lesion, vertical deviation worse in lateral gaze, often non-comitant.
Usually primary vertical, horizontal changes are secondary.
Dissociated Vertical Deviation (DVD)
Slow, upward drift of one eye when covered, exycloduction, often bilateral but asymmetric.
Primarily vertical deviation, does not typically manifest as A/V horizontal patterns.
Cyclovertical Muscle Palsies
Significant vertical deviation, fundus torsion, head tilt, may have secondary horizontal components.
Pattern is secondary to primary vertical/torsional defect, not the main feature.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading of Patterns
content: **Significant A-Pattern:** Difference of ≥10 prism diopters (PD) between upgaze and downgaze.
**Significant V-Pattern:** Difference of ≥15 prism diopters (PD) between upgaze and downgaze.
**Mild/Moderate/Severe:** Can be further graded based on the magnitude of PD difference, e.g., mild (10-15 PD), moderate (15-25 PD), severe (>25 PD).
**Primary Deviation:** The pattern is superimposed on a primary horizontal deviation (e.g., esotropia, exotropia).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment: Surgical Indications
content: **Cosmetic Improvement:** Significant eye turn that bothers the patient or family.
**Elimination of Abnormal Head Posture:** To achieve comfortable binocular vision.
**Relief of Diplopia/Asthenopia:** Symptoms interfering with daily activities.
**Improvement of Binocular Vision:** Expanding the field of single vision.
**Prevention/Treatment of Amblyopia:** In pediatric cases.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: General Principles
content: **Principle 1: Address Oblique Muscle Dysfunction** – Weaken overacting obliques, strengthen underacting obliques.
**Principle 2: Vertically Transpose Horizontal Rectus Muscles** – Shift the insertion of MR/LR to change their action in upgaze/downgaze.
**Principle 3: Address Primary Horizontal Deviation** – Recession/Resection of horizontal recti as indicated.
**Principle 4: Adjustable Sutures** – Can be used in adults for fine-tuning postoperative alignment.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Over/Undercorrection:** Residual pattern or horizontal deviation.
**Consecutive Deviation:** Esotropia becoming exotropia, or vice versa.
**New Patterns:** Unmasking of a different pattern or vertical deviation.
**Diplopia:** Especially if fusion was poor pre-op or surgical outcome is imprecise.
**Anterior Segment Ischemia:** Rare, with multiple rectus muscle surgeries.
**Adverse Oblique Muscle Effects:** E.g., Brown's syndrome-like restriction after SO tuck, or IO palsy after recession/myectomy.
**Prognosis:** Generally good for achieving functional alignment, though some residual incomitance may persist.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Acute Onset Strabismus:** Especially with diplopia, requires urgent neurological evaluation to rule out cranial nerve palsies, intracranial mass, or ischemia.
**Associated Neurological Symptoms:** Headache, weakness, numbness, visual field defects.
**Painful Eye Movements:** Suggestive of inflammation or orbital pathology.
**Significant Vertical Deviation:** May indicate a more complex etiology than just A/V patterns.
**Profound Vision Loss:** Unexplained by strabismus alone.

content.explanation: **V**-Pattern, **I**nferior Oblique (IO) weakening (recession/myectomy), **L**ateral recti (LR) shifted **U**p (for V-ET) or **M**edial recti (MR) shifted **U**p (for V-XT). **A**-Pattern, **S**uperior Oblique (SO) weakening (tenotomy/tenectomy), **L**ateral recti (LR) shifted **D**own (for A-ET) or **M**edial recti (MR) shifted **D**own (for A-XT).

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always measure deviation in primary, upgaze, and downgaze to detect patterns.
Fundus torsion can be a helpful, albeit indirect, sign of oblique muscle dysfunction (extorsion with IO overaction, intorsion with SO overaction).
Weakening overacting oblique muscles is often the most effective way to correct an A or V pattern.
Vertical transposition of horizontal recti should only be performed for significant patterns (≥10/15 PD difference) and is usually combined with recession/resection.
For every 1mm of vertical transposition, approximately 2-3 PD of pattern correction is achieved.
V-patterns are more common than A-patterns in both esotropia and exotropia.
Chin-up posture often indicates V-exotropia or A-esotropia (to utilize upgaze where deviation is less). Chin-down posture suggests V-esotropia or A-exotropia (to utilize downgaze).

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances focus on refining surgical dosages, understanding the role of orbital connective tissue and muscle pulleys (active pulley hypothesis) in pattern strabismus, and the increasing use of adjustable sutures to achieve precise alignment in adults. Studies like those by Scott, Parks, and Wright have significantly contributed to our understanding and management of oblique muscle dysfunction and pattern strabismus, emphasizing quantitative measurements and tailored surgical approaches.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Amblyopia Risk:** High in young children with constant strabismus; requires prompt detection and treatment (patching, atropine).
**Sensory Adaptation:** Children often adapt by developing suppression, making diplopia less common.
**Timing of Surgery:** Early surgery in infants with large deviations can improve the chances of developing some binocularity.
**Developmental Impact:** Uncorrected patterns can affect academic performance due to reading difficulties (e.g., A-pattern esotropia in downgaze).
**Syndromic Associations:** A/V patterns can be associated with certain syndromes (e.g., craniofacial dysostoses), necessitating a multidisciplinary approach.
